title: A tight band with new arrangements every week
summary: The band played together constantly and learned brand-new charts from studio arrangers who dropped by the Onyx, reading music off their knees; it ended with the war.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: That's right. We did a tremendous amount of playing together. We practically -- well, not lived together, but we saw a great deal of each other, and it got to the point where this music we played -- and it was all with your head in the charts, everything was with your head in the charts, because everything was -- you know, it wasn't like we'd play one -- you know, like most bands, they'd have about

10 or 12 numbers that they'd play and play and play, so that's why they get to know them. Then you'd just play them. But we had a tremendous amount of music which was brand new, and the -- and the thing was that there were some arrangements that we got a week before that we'd play them, you know, like in the Onyx Club. Then it got so that -- like I stated before, these fellows who, you know, were staff arrangers at the studio. Radio then, it wasn't television. They would come, you know, and everybody came for a second and they'd sit there and drink and listen to us play, and they'd get an idea and they'd make this arrangement and bring it to us, just to see how we'd play it, maybe if we could play it, and how it would sound and all that sort of thing. And we'd take them and just pass them out and play them. You know?

I remember we didn't even have music stands. I'd cross my legs just like this and lay the sheet on my knee and play it. Yeah. Yeah. It was -- it was a very successful, I would say, operation. But it came to an abrupt end with -- when the war started.
